subcategory: East Asian ornamental-edible stone fruit tree

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in full sun in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil; Matsubara Red opens its fully double, blood-red flowers very early, often while still in the grip of winter, so a site sheltered from harsh wind helps protect the bloom.

directions: Matsubara Red is grown chiefly for having the darkest, most saturated red flowers among commercially available Japanese flowering apricots, with small, fully double blossoms opening on bare branches ahead of the foliage. Like other mume cultivars it forms an upright, vase-shaped small tree and sets the typical sour, apricot-like fruit, but gardeners select it almost entirely for the intensity of its winter color rather than for a culinary crop. It has been grown in North American nurseries since at least the 1970s and performs best with an open, airy canopy maintained by pruning right after bloom. Give it full sun and well-drained, slightly acidic soil, and it will reward a cold, bare winter garden with an unusually vivid display.

common_name: W.B. Clarke Weeping Japanese Flowering Apricot
subcategory: East Asian ornamental-edible stone fruit tree

planting.note: Plant grafted specimens in spring in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil; the cascading branches benefit from a raised site or small mound so the weeping habit can be seen fully from below.

directions: W.B. Clarke is the classic weeping-form Japanese flowering apricot, named for California nurseryman Walter Bosworth Clarke, whose San Jose nursery introduced several notable mume selections in the early twentieth century. Its branches arch and cascade downward from the point of grafting, and in late winter they are lined with fragrant, fully double pink flowers that give the whole tree the look of a blossoming fountain. Because the habit is entirely dependent on the graft, it is typically trained as a small specimen or accent tree rather than planted in groups, and staking while young helps establish a clean trunk before the weeping growth takes over. Prune lightly right after flowering to remove crossing branches and keep the cascade from dragging on the ground.

subcategory: East Asian ornamental-edible stone fruit tree

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in full sun in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil; the huge, ruffled flowers open in mid-to-late winter and carry a strong, sweet fragrance that can perfume a whole garden corner.

directions: Dawn carries unusually large, ruffled, fully double pink flowers that are among the showiest of any Japanese flowering apricot, and it was renamed from an older Japanese cultivar around 1929 by W.B. Clarke's California nursery. The blossoms open on bare wood in the depths of winter and are heavily, sweetly scented, making it a favorite for planting near a path, window, or seating area where the fragrance can be enjoyed up close. Like other mume cultivars it forms a rounded, small-to-medium tree and will set small sour fruit, though it is grown almost entirely for its flower display. Prune to an open form right after bloom to let light and air into the canopy and encourage strong flowering the following winter.

subcategory: East Asian ornamental-edible stone fruit tree

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in full sun in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil; Bonita's semi-double rose-red flowers open on bare branches in late winter ahead of the foliage.

directions: Bonita bears semi-double, rose-red blossoms on an upright, vase-shaped tree, and the cultivar was named in 1940 by the W.B. Clarke nursery of San Jose, California, reportedly after one of the nurseryman's three daughters. The flowers open in late winter while the branches are still bare, giving a strong wash of warm color at a time when little else is blooming, and the small sour fruit that follows is typical of the species rather than a feature of the selection. It shares the species' long lifespan and gnarled, picturesque mature form, so an open site with room to develop is worth planning for from the start. Grow it in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil and prune lightly after flowering to maintain an airy canopy.

subcategory: East Asian ornamental-edible stone fruit tree

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in full sun in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil; Kobai's deep pink, almost red, double flowers have made it one of the most widely favored mume cultivars across East Asia.

directions: Kobai, whose name translates roughly as 'crimson plum,' is an old Japanese cultivar prized for very deep double pink flowers that read as nearly pure red from a distance, opening in the heart of winter around the time of the Lunar New Year in much of its native range. It has been grown in North American gardens since at least the early 1990s and forms the same upright, long-lived small tree typical of the species, eventually developing the gnarled, picturesque trunk mume is known for with age. The intensity of its color makes it a popular choice for Japanese-style gardens where a single winter-flowering specimen is meant to anchor the whole composition. Plant in full sun in well-drained, slightly acidic soil and prune after bloom to keep the canopy open for next winter's flower display.

subcategory: East Asian ornamental-edible stone fruit tree

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in full sun in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil; Omoi-no-mama is notable for opening white, pink, and pink-flushed flowers together on the same tree, giving rise to its Japanese name, which translates loosely as 'as one pleases.'

directions: Omoi-no-mama is one of the most distinctive Japanese flowering apricot cultivars because individual flowers on the same branch can open white, pale pink, or flushed with deeper pink, so no two seasons of bloom look quite identical. The semi-double flowers carry a light almond-like fragrance and open on bare wood in late winter, and the cultivar has long been one of the more widely grown ume selections in Japan as well as in Western botanic garden collections. It forms a somewhat smaller, more rounded tree than many mume cultivars, making it a reasonable choice where space is tighter than a full-size specimen requires. Grow it in full sun in well-drained, slightly acidic soil and prune right after flowering to maintain an open form.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist to dry, well-drained soil in full sun; Hiwassee was selected for cold tolerance well beyond the typical range of southern wax myrtle and makes a good tall evergreen screen in cooler zones than the species normally tolerates.

directions: Hiwassee is a cold-hardy wax myrtle selection that traces back to a plant growing in University of Tennessee trial gardens, where it survived temperatures around minus four degrees Fahrenheit with only minor leaf burn, well beyond what the species typically endures. Unlike the several dwarf and compact wax myrtle selections already common in cultivation, Hiwassee keeps the larger, fast-growing habit of the wild species, making it suited to a tall informal hedge, windbreak, or small evergreen tree rather than a foundation planting. Its narrow, aromatic, gray-green leaves stay evergreen through winter, and female plants produce the small blue-gray waxy berries typical of the species, valuable to overwintering songbirds. It tolerates heat, drought, salt spray, and poor soil, and asks for little beyond full sun and room to reach its larger mature size.

North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Rubra is a male clone selected for its brick-red flower buds and reddish winter stems, and, being male, never sets fruit.

directions: Rubra is a male-flowered spicebush selection, traced to a plant found near Hopkinton, Rhode Island, chosen for flower buds and winter twigs with a noticeably deeper brick-red cast than the typical species. In early spring, clusters of small flowers open along the bare stems ahead of the leaves, giving a stronger, warmer-toned early display than seed-grown spicebush, though as a male clone it never produces the ornamental red berries female plants carry. Like the species, its aromatic foliage turns clear gold in autumn and serves as a larval host for spicebush swallowtail butterflies. Because it is useful specifically as a reliable pollen source, pair it with a known female spicebush or selection where berry production in the garden is wanted, and give it the same moist, humus-rich, shaded site the species prefers.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Green Gold is a male clone selected for unusually large, showy yellow flower clusters and, like other male spicebush, does not fruit.

directions: Green Gold is a male spicebush selection grown specifically for its flowers, which open in very early spring in noticeably larger, showier yellow clusters than the species typically produces, making the early bloom display more conspicuous in the still-bare woodland understory. As a male clone it sets no berries, so it is planted purely for ornament and as a dependable pollen source rather than for fall fruit. It carries the same spicy-fragrant foliage as the species when crushed, the same clear yellow fall color, and the same value as a larval host for spicebush swallowtail caterpillars. Site it in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to shade, ideally within range of a female spicebush if berries are desired elsewhere in the planting.
